evidence.label: Vanishing of higher bounded Hochschild cohomology

headline: Proves bounded Hochschild cohomology of every von Neumann algebra vanishes in degrees two and up, settling Kadison–Ringrose.
scope: Bounded multilinear Hochschild cocycles of degree at least two on any complex von Neumann algebra, with values in the algebra itself.
plain: A von Neumann algebra is a family of operators closed under sums, products and a strong kind of limit. A cocycle is a multi-input map that satisfies a fixed cancellation rule, and the easy ones come from simpler maps one level down. Kadison and Ringrose conjectured that every bounded cocycle is one of the easy ones. Degree one was settled in 1966 by Kadison and Sakai. This paper proves every higher degree, with no extra conditions on the algebra, and Lean checks it.
doesNot: This does not reprove the degree-one inner-derivation theorem; it relies on that earlier result for degree one.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: The self-coefficient cohomology question, which Sinclair and Smith trace to 1967; Kadison and Ringrose developed the higher-degree theory
scorecard.significanceWhy: It settles the Kadison–Ringrose cohomology conjecture for all von Neumann algebras, with a Lean check of the higher degrees.

explanation:
Take 2-by-2 matrices and write e11, e12, e21 for the matrices with a single 1 in that position. Fix b = e11 and set D(a) = ab − ba. Then D(e12) = e12·e11 − e11·e12 = 0 − e12 = −e12. Also D(e21) = e21 and D(e11) = 0. Check the product rule D(xy) = xD(y) + D(x)y with x = e12 and y = e21. The left side is D(e11) = 0. The right side is e12·e21 − e12·e21 = e11 − e11 = 0. They agree.

A map with that product rule is a derivation. The rule is the degree-one cocycle equation. A cocycle is a bounded map of k inputs whose Hochschild differential, a fixed alternating sum, is zero[3]. Bounded means it stretches inputs by at most a fixed factor. Cocycles of the form D(a) = ab − ba come from one element b, one degree lower. Such cocycles are called coboundaries, or inner when k = 1. Bounded Hochschild cohomology in degree k measures cocycles that are not coboundaries. When it is zero, every cocycle equation has a bounded solution one degree down.

The algebras here are von Neumann algebras: families of operators on a Hilbert space, closed under sums, products, adjoints and pointwise limits. Kadison and Sakai showed every derivation of such an algebra into itself is inner[4]. The Kadison–Ringrose conjecture asks the same in every degree[2]. Earlier work settled many cases: type I and hyperfinite algebras, algebras with a Cartan subalgebra, and factors with property Γ[5,6]. The obstacle was the general type II₁ case, with no extra structure to average over.

A primitive is a map one degree lower whose differential is the cocycle. The paper proves every bounded cocycle of degree at least two has a bounded primitive[1]. It needs no separability or type restriction. The key step averages one input over a single random walk on the algebra's unitaries, the operators that preserve length[7]. Averaging gives a harmonic map, one equal to its own average. A new Liouville theorem shows such a map must have the simple form T(x) = T(1)x[8]. Together with the degree-one theorem, this settles the conjecture positively[9].

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, has a formal statement of the main theorem: every bounded cocycle of degree at least two has a bounded primitive. The degree-one theorem is outside that statement, but it is a 1966 result. So the paper proves the higher-degree theorem, as far as the Lean statement matches the paper. No specialist review is published.
hypeCheck: Landmark-level claim with a Lean check of every degree from two up. Degree one rests on the 1966 Kadison–Sakai theorem. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A family of operators on a Hilbert space closed under sums, products, adjoints and pointwise limits.
A linear map D with the product rule D(xy) = xD(y) + D(x)y.
A derivation of the form D(a) = ab − ba for one fixed element b.
A map of k inputs whose Hochschild differential, a fixed alternating sum built from products, is zero.
A map g of one fewer input whose differential dg equals the given cocycle.
The bounded degree-k cocycles modulo those with a bounded primitive; zero means every cocycle has one.
A class of von Neumann algebras with a finite trace and no minimal projections; the hardest case here.
An operator U with U*U = UU* = 1, so it preserves lengths.
